name: BoolQ
description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer that is either 'yes' or 'no'.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions.
rai:dataCollection: We gather data using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ), with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator. Annotators first decide if the question is good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information, before seeing the Wikipedia page. For good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, may mark questions as not answerable if the article does not contain the requested information, and finally mark whether the answer is yes or no. The dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set, for a total of 16k questions.
rai:dataCollectionType: Passive Data Collection, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources are anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages/articles returned among the first five search results. The final examples use selected paragraphs from Wikipedia articles and include the article title.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Unlike in NQ, the dataset only uses questions that were marked as having a yes/no answer, and pairs each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document. The authors combine 13k newly gathered questions with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set, then split the 16k questions into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically filtered using a manually constructed set of indicator first words and a sufficient-length requirement. Questions are only retained if a Wikipedia page appears in the first five search results. During annotation, only questions judged good are kept, and only those marked as having a yes/no answer are used. Each question is paired with the selected answer-containing passage rather than the full document to reduce ambiguity and keep inputs small enough for existing entailment models.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: first they decide whether the question is good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information, before seeing the Wikipedia page; next, for good questions, they find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, or mark it as not answerable if the article does not contain the requested information; finally, they mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. To assess annotation quality, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: On 110 randomly chosen examples, answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels created by three authors. Of the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the authors used singly annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets to gather a larger dataset.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Human annotators; three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples for quality assessment.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that the data and code are presented at https://goo.gl/boolq. It also notes that the dataset had been updated since one analysis was carried out, but no maintenance schedule or deprecation policy is provided.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions. The authors argue that naturally occurring yes/no questions have the benefit of being very challenging while remaining tied to an obvious end-use application, rather than an artificial setting.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common, with 62.31% in the train set. The paper also notes some correlation between question topic or type and the likelihood of a yes answer, and that some language patterns in passages may correlate with the answer. Questions are gathered only when a Wikipedia page appears among the first five Google search results, and topics often include entertainment media, sports, and other popular topics.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset uses singly annotated examples in the main splits, and annotation errors and ambiguous or debatable cases exist. Annotating is expensive because annotators must search entire Wikipedia documents and read carefully. The dataset pairs questions with selected passages instead of full documents, which reduces ambiguity but limits the task to passage-level evidence. The analysis of inference types may be slightly out of date because the dataset was updated after that analysis. The authors also note that none of the models in the paper use the article titles, although titles are included.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a reading comprehension and yes/no question answering benchmark to test inferential natural language understanding. It is split into training, development, and test sets: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test. The paper uses it for model training, fine-tuning, development, testing, transfer learning experiments, and evaluation of human and model accuracy.
